To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) chemotherapy-induced cytopenias can be anticipated and monitored, (ii) the nadir of cytopenias is usually predictable, (iii) transfusions should be used to treat symptomatic patients, (iv) prophylactic transfusions should not be routinely used, and (v) prophylactic granulocyte transfusion therapy is rarely indicated.

the most important factor for the development of chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia is the dose of chemotherapy and the most important factor in the prevention of chemotherapy-induced thromboembolism is prophylactic use of low-molecular-weight heparin.

the management of chemotherapy-induced bone marrow supression in cancer is to monitor the nadir of cytopenias and to provide symptomatic relief.

the use of growth factors is not indicated for the routine prophylaxis of neutropenic fever in cancer patients.
the use of prophylactic antibiotics in patients with neutropenia is not recommended.
